4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163	
164	## Finish
165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	ABSTRACTBackgroundHeterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the tumour necrosis factor alpha induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) gene cause an early-onset auto-inflammatory disease named haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20). Here we describe three unrelated patients with autoimmune lupus nephritis (LN) phenotypes carrying three novel mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene.MethodsWhole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to identify the causative mutations in three biopsy-proven LN patients. Sanger sequencing and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) were used to validate the mutations identified by WES. RNA sequencing, qPCR and cytometric bead array was used to detect inflammatory signatures in the patients.ResultsThe patients predominantly presented with an autoimmune phenotype, including autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, multipositive autoantibodies and LN. Additionally, novel phenotypes of allergy and pericardial effusion were first reported. WES identified three novel heterozygous mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene, including a novel splicing mutation located in the canonical splicing site (c.634+2T>C) resulting in an intron 4 insertion containing a premature stop codon, a de novo novel copy number variation (exon 7–8 deletion) and a novel nonsense mutation c.1300_1301delinsTA causing a premature stop codon. We further identified hyperactivation signatures of nuclear factor- kappa B and type I IFN signalling and overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the blood. This report expanded the phenotype to a later age, as two girls were diagnosed at age 3 years and one man at age 29 years.ConclusionsKidney involvement may be the main feature of the clinical spectrum of HA20, even in adults. Genetic screening should be considered for early-onset LN patients.

14	## INTRODUCTION
15	
16	The A20 protein, encoded by the tumour necrosis factor alpha induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) gene, is a negative regulator of the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signalling pathway. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene cause haploinsufficiency of A20 [HA20; Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) 616744], characterized by an early-onset auto-inflammatory disease [1]. The major phenotype of HA20 is Behçet-like symptoms, including recurrent aphthous stomatitis, genital ulcers and intestinal symptoms [2]. However, HA20 was also identified in patients with childhood-onset autoimmune diseases and autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome [1, 3]. To date, the predominant autoimmune phenotype associated with HA20 may vary in family members carrying the same mutation.
17	
18	Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE; OMIM 152700) is one of the most heterogeneous systemic autoimmune diseases and presents great challenges in diagnosis and treatment. To develop innovative therapies, a better understanding of SLE pathogenesis is needed. Multiple genetic factors are presumed to be involved in SLE. For example, genome-wide association studies have identified a number of common alleles, including TNFAIP3 gene polymorphisms, which increase the risk of developing lupus [4–7]. In addition, >30 causative genes for monogenic SLE and lupus-like syndrome have been described, which are associated with complement components, type I interferon, NF-κB, self-tolerance and other pathways that have yet to be characterized [8–13]. Although the proportion of patients with monogenic SLE is small, they provide considerable insight into signalling pathways contributing the SLE phenotype. Discovery of shared autoimmunity pathways in SLE can provide clues for better understanding of this complex disorder, its prognosis and new therapeutic approaches.
19	
20	In this study we identified by whole-exome sequencing (WES), three novel mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene leading to a predominantly lupus nephritis (LN) phenotype. We further confirmed the hyperactivation signatures of NF-κB and type I interferon (IFN) signalling and overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines. The results expand the genotypic and phenotypic spectrums of TNFAIP3-associated disease. They provide evidence to highlight the need to consider genetic screening in early-onset SLE patients as well as in sporadic adult patients.

25	
26	Three biopsy-proven LN patients with TNFAIP3 loss-of-function mutations were studied. Six adult controls were healthy colleagues in our laboratory, including three males and three females. The age range was 24–34 years. Three male children as controls (0–3 years old) underwent routine physical examination in the clinic. All subjects or their guardians provided written informed consent in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration for enrolment in research protocols approved by Jinling Hospital, Children's Hospital of Fudan University or Jilin University.
27	
28	### WES
29	
30	Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood using the Chemagic DNA Blood 3K Kit Special H24 (CMG-1073; PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA). One microgram of DNA was used for WES at BGI, Shenzhen, China. All genes across the whole-exome regions were explored. For patient 1 (P1), variants were annotated by Annotate Variation (ANNOVAR) software. Candidate variants were filtered to remove those presenting in the gnomAD, Kaviar, dbSNP and an in-house database and further filtered by dominant inheritance. For patient 2 (P2) and patient 3 (P3), WES was performed and analysed concurrently for the proband and both parents. Other family members were tested by Sanger sequencing for the presence or absence of the variants identified in the probands.
31	
32	### Assessment of the splicing mutation in P1
33	
34	The PAXgene Blood RNA Kit (762174; Qiagen, Venlo, The Netherlands) was used for the purification of intracellular RNA from whole blood of P1 collected in the PAXgene Blood RNA tube. The cDNA was synthesized using the PrimeScript Reverse Transcriptase kit with gDNA Eraser (RR047A; Takara Bio, Shiga, Japan). Then a set of specific primers for exon 3 and exon 7 was used to assess the effect of the splice-site variant in intron 4.
35	
36	### Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assay
37	
38	One microgram of RNA was used for cDNA synthesis. qPCR was performed using TB Green Premix Ex Taq II (RR820A; Takara). The reactions were run on a LightCycler 480 Instrument II (Roche, Indianapolis, IN, USA). Relative mRNA expression was normalized to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and analysed by the 2^–ΔΔCt method.
39	
40	### Copy number variant analysis by qPCR
41	
42	Copy number variant (CNV) of the TNFAIP3 gene identified in P2 by WES was validated by qPCR, which was performed as described earlier with specific primers for exons 5–9.
43	
44	### RNA sequencing
45	
46	One microgram of RNA was used for library preparation using NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) following the manufacturer's recommendations. Index codes were added to attribute sequences to each sample. The libraries were sequenced on a Novaseq (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and 150-bp paired-end reads were generated. Sequenced reads were mapped against the human reference genome (GRCh38) using HISAT2. The tool featureCounts was used to count the read numbers mapped to each gene. Differential expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 R package.
47	
48	### Cytokine detection in serum
49	
50	The serum concentrations of cytokines were measured by cytometric bead array. All data were analysed by FCAPArray version 3 software (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA).

156	### Activation of inflammatory signalling
157	
158	Table 3 summarizes the immunologic characteristics of the patients. All were strongly positive for ANA and/or anti-dsDNA and had decreased C3 and C4 levels. Additionally, P2 and P3 had increased CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) without infection. IgE levels of P1 and P2 were increased.
159	
160	To investigate their inflammatory signature, we performed RNA sequencing using RNA extracted from whole blood cells of P1. The gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed activation of the inflammatory response, such as NF-κB, Toll-like receptor and tumour necrosis factor (TNF) signalling pathways (Fig. 4A–D). A20 is a potent inhibitor of the NF-κB pathway. As expected, we observed significant up-regulation of NF-κB signalling compared to three controls (Fig. 4E). A20 also can inhibit the retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA-5) pathway and restrict the activation of type I IFN. A strong type I IFN signature is observed in whole blood cells of P1 compared with controls (Fig. 4F). The 28-gene IFN score confirmed the activation of type I IFN signalling (Fig. 4G). qPCR confirmed the up-regulation of IFN-stimulated genes in P1’s whole blood cells, such as IFIT1, IFI44L, RSAD2, ISG15, OAS1, and MX2 (Fig. 4H). The serum cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6) was also significantly elevated compared with controls (Fig. 4I). Together, our results indicated that both NF-κB and type I IFN pathways were activated when A20 was deficient.

164	### Treatments and outcomes
165	
166	All patients received steroids and two patients also received mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and/or tacrolimus or cyclosporine A. Belimumab, a human monoclonal antibody targeting B-cell activating factor and the Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor tofacitinib were also used (Table 4). His condition gradually improved, as autoantibodies turned negative, complement levels returned to normal and proteinuria decreased. Methylprednisolone pulse therapy and methylprednisolone with cyclosporine were successively prescribed to P2. Later, belimumab was added because of the high titres of autoantibodies. Her proteinuria, complement levels and autoantibodies quickly returned to normal. P3 received four rounds of methylprednisolone pulse therapy then prednisone, hydroxychloroquine, and the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib were used. During follow-up, she had no fever or proteinuria. Her haemoglobin returned to normal and hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy improved.

212	## DISCUSSION
213	
214	In the current study we described the clinical and pathological features of three patients carrying novel mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene leading to HA20. HA20 classically presents with auto-inflammatory features. In contrast, our patients were predominantly characterized by autoimmune features with LN.
215	
216	The first mutation, c.634+2T>C,  affects the splicing of mRNA and creates a frameshift mutation that removes both the ovarian tumour (OTU) domain and all zinc finger domains. The second mutation, exon 7–8 deletion, results in the absence of the OTU domain proximal to the zinc finger domains and zinc finger domains 1–5. The third mutation, c.1300_1301delinsTA (p. A434*), results in a premature stop codon that removes zinc finger domains 2–7. They all lead to the truncating of the A20 protein. Previous molecular and biochemical studies showed that truncating mutations of A20 protein, even only the seventh (last) zinc finger domain, correlated with HA20 clinical disease as well as diminished A20 expression and suppressive activity, leading to increased TNF-α-associated NF-κB activity [1, 16, 17]. Similar findings of obvious activation of the NF-κB pathway were observed in our patients.
217	
218	In addition to expanding of genotypic spectrum, we reported for the first time an allergy history in P1 and massive pericardial effusion in P2 associated with TNFAIP3 mutation. Additionally, P1 was adult onset, different from previous reports. These are novel phenotypes. All three patients met the classification criteria for SLE [18] and were biopsy-proven LN. They shared some clinical hallmarks with auto-inflammatory phenotype of HA20 [1, 2, 15], including recurrent oral ulcers, intermittent fever, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, arthralgia or arthritis and elevated pro-inflammatory markers. They also presented with distinct autoimmune features, including autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, multiple positive autoantibodies, decreased complement levels and immune-complex deposits in the kidneys. Therefor the study expands both the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of TNFAIP3-associated disease.
219	
220	While >36 unique TNFAIP3 mutations that are associated with auto-inflammatory and autoimmune disease have been collected in the Infevers database, only 2 mutations were associated with renal involvement, including a p.Q187* mutation in a proliferative glomerulonephritis (class III) patient and a p.F224Sfs*4 mutation in a membranous lupus (class V) patient [2, 19]. The three particular novel mutations in our patients were associated with LN. Whether the particular mutations are associated with organ-specific manifestations is currently unknown. More cases are needed in further studies.
221	
222	HA20 is commonly reported in early-onset patients [15, 20]. However, P1 in our study was adult onset. Manifestations and disease courses were quite different among the three patients, suggesting other possible genetic and environmental factors. Additionally, P3’s mother had a corresponding mutation but is still asymptomatic, suggesting a significant degree of variable expressivity and reduced penetrance in HA20 patients.
223	
224	For P2, an auto-inflammatory phenotype was predominant in the first year of her illness, without any autoantibodies. Then weak autoantibodies appeared and progressed to a strong autoimmune phenotype. The transition from auto-inflammatory to autoimmune disorder suggested the dysregulation of immune homeostasis. A20 is an anti-inflammatory molecule that restricts multiple intracellular signalling cascades in multiple cell types including myeloid cells, dendritic cells (DCs), B cells and intestinal epithelial cells [21]. Mice with B-cell-specific ablation of A20 spontaneously developed an autoimmune condition similar to human SLE, whereas intestinal cell–specific A20 deficiency resulted in intestinal inflammation [22, 23]. Further, two independent DC A20-deficient mouse strains showed remarkably different phenotypes. One strain developed SLE-like symptoms, including the presence of anti-dsDNA autoantibody, glomerulonephritis, antiphospholipid syndrome and arthritis [24]. In contrast, the other strain spontaneously developed colitis, seronegative ankylosing arthritis and enthesitis [25]. Therefore A20 may regulate crucial steps in immune cell homeostasis and additional factors such as major affected cell types, genetic backgrounds and the environment may play a determinative role in the disease phenotype.
225	
226	Autoimmune features were reported in aging TNFAIP3 knockout mice [26]. Autoimmunity is considered a complication of HA20 with aging and/or the accumulation of other genetic factors [27]. However, two patients (P2 and P3) showed marked autoimmunity at a very early age (<3 year) and P3 showed obvious autoimmune characteristics from the onset. Therefore the trigger factor of auto-inflammatory or autoimmune cannot be simply attributed to aging. By screening the common SLE risk alleles in the WES data, we found that several common SLE risk alleles may have contributed to disease expressivity [6, 28–31]. Analysing the combined effect of rare and common gene variants in LN may shed light on interactions between signalling pathways and may further reveal potential therapeutic targets.
227	
228	LN pathogenesis is associated with immune complex deposition within the kidney as well as activation of resident cell types, infiltration of immune cells and expression of inflammatory cytokines [32]. Many of these inflammatory mediators are the result of activation of the NF-κB pathway, which is a key transcription factor for maturation of DCs, activation and differentiation of T-cells, survival and recruitment of neutrophils and inflammatory signalling and polarization within macrophages [33]. Blocking classical NF-κB signalling markedly abrogated disease, with an improvement in proteinuria, kidney function and histopathology [34]. In addition, type I IFN may drive the pathogenesis of LN and is associated with disease flares [35]. Single-cell studies also demonstrate high type I IFN signatures in LN patients [36]. A20 not only inhibits NF-κB signalling by modifying ubiquitylated protein substrates in multiple ways, but also blocks type I IFN signalling by removing K63-linked ubiquitin chains from TBK1/IKKi, which is activated by the RIG-I/MDA5–mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein axis [21]. 230	Biologics targeting cytokines are commonly used as novel treatments because of excessive production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in HA20 patients [1, 27, 37]. For example, anti-TNF, anti-IL-1β and anti-IL-6 agents can effectively inhibit systemic inflammatory responses in these patients [2, 38]. Other immunotherapies, such as anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies and JAK inhibitors, have also been reported as useful [39–41]. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be considered for patients with refractory disease [39]. Genetic screening of patients based on clinical characteristics alone is unlikely to be sensitive enough to detect all relevant cases. Next-generation sequencing, like WES/whole-genomic sequencing, combined with RNA sequencing is a powerful tool to identify pathogenic TNFAIP3 mutations and potential novel pathogenic genes in patients with LN [42–44].

234	In summary, we report the clinical manifestations and immunological characteristics of three biopsy-proven LN patients with novel pathogenic mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene. Continuous improvement and widespread application of genetic testing technology provide new diagnostic and therapeutic options for autoimmune diseases. Monogenic diseases, such as HA20, may help advance our understanding of disease pathogenesis and develop targeted therapies for more common, multifactorial disorders with lupus-like manifestations.
